name: Jesus
info: Jesus was a Jewish preacher and religious leader of Galilee and Judaea in the first century, whom Christians hold to be the Messiah and the Son of God and from whose followers Christianity grew.

facts.born: c. 6 to 4 BCE, traditionally at Bethlehem, raised at Nazareth in Galilee; a Jew, the son of Mary and her husband Joseph
facts.died: 30 or 33 CE at Jerusalem, crucified on the order of Pontius Pilate according to the Gospels and most historians; the Quran holds that he was not killed but raised into Heaven
facts.role: Itinerant teacher in Galilee and Judaea; Christians hold him to be the Messiah (the Christ) and, in most branches, God the Son; Muslims regard him as a prophet and the messiah; historians describe a Jewish preacher and the founder of a renewal movement within Judaism
facts.known: teaching in parables about the Kingdom of God; the twelve apostles; healings and exorcisms; the Sermon on the Mount; crucifixion under Pontius Pilate; the Resurrection, held by Christians as the foundation of the Church; the central figure of Christianity

t: Jesus was a Jewish teacher of Galilee who taught in parables about the Kingdom of God, gathered followers and appointed twelve of them as apostles.
The Gospels tell that he was arrested in Jerusalem and crucified on the order of Pontius Pilate; historians count his baptism and crucifixion among the best attested facts about him.
Christians hold that he rose from the dead, and that belief became the foundation of the early Church, while Judaism, Islam and other faiths each give him a different place.
dyk: The Gospels give about one third of their text to the last week of Jesus's life in Jerusalem, and Matthew and Luke give two genealogies for him that differ almost entirely after King David.
ev: Jesus is born, in the Gospels' accounts during the reign of Herod the Great
Baptized by John the Baptist, he begins his ministry in Galilee, according to one common estimate
He appoints twelve apostles and teaches in parables, including the Sermon on the Mount
He travels to Jerusalem for Passover, enters the city and drives the money changers from the Temple
After a last meal with his twelve apostles he is arrested, brought before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin and handed to Pilate
He is crucified, with Pilate's inscription reading King of the Jews; the date is 30 or 33 CE
His followers report his empty tomb and appearances, and the Acts of the Apostles places his ascension forty days later

sections.early:
Jesus was a Jew born about the beginning of the first century. Most scholars give a birth between 6 and 4 BCE, because Matthew places it in the reign of Herod the Great, who died around 4 BCE. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke say that his mother Mary was a virgin who conceived through the Holy Spirit and that he was born in Bethlehem. They give two genealogies that differ markedly after David. Some scholars, among them Gerd Theissen and Annette Merz, conclude that he was born in Nazareth and that the Bethlehem story was developed to fit scripture. Most scholars regard the birth narratives of Matthew and Luke as the clearest cases of invention in the Gospel accounts, while conservative scholars such as Ben Witherington argue that they trace back to much earlier traditions.

The Gospels name Nazareth in Galilee as his home. His other family members included four brothers, James, Joses, Judas and Simon, and unnamed sisters. Mark calls him a tektōn, traditionally translated as carpenter. He was probably able to read and debate scripture. Most scholars hold that he spoke Aramaic in its Galilean form and perhaps some Greek. Judaea had become a Roman province in 6 CE, while Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, and many Jews looked for deliverance from their pagan rulers.
sections.rise:
The Synoptic Gospels place the start of Jesus's ministry at his baptism in the River Jordan by John the Baptist, who preached repentance and foretold someone more powerful. In Mark, the Spirit descends on Jesus like a dove and a voice from heaven declares him God's Son, and he is then tempted by Satan in the wilderness for forty days. Most modern scholars regard the baptism as historical, since early Christians would hardly have invented a story that might suggest Jesus needed to repent.

Luke dates John's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and scholars arrive at about 28 or 29 CE for the start of Jesus's ministry, with other approaches giving 27 to 29. After John's arrest he preached in Galilee. The Gospels tell that he called his first disciples, fishermen, who left their nets to follow him, and then appointed twelve apostles. Luke adds a larger group of disciples and the sending out of 70 or 72 in pairs to prepare the towns he planned to visit. In John the first two apostles are initially disciples of John the Baptist, who calls Jesus the Lamb of God.
sections.deeds:
In the Synoptics Jesus teaches about the Kingdom of God, often in parables, which make up about a third of his recorded teaching. He calls people to repent and to devote themselves wholly to God, and when asked for the greatest commandment he names love of God and love of neighbour. His other teachings include loving enemies, forgiving those who have sinned, and turning the other cheek. The Sermon on the Mount in Matthew and the Sermon on the Plain in Luke gather many of these sayings. Some contemporaries thought he broke the law, for instance on the Sabbath.

The Gospels describe healings, exorcisms, the raising of the dead and nature miracles such as turning water into wine, and Christians hold these to be acts of divine power. Jesus says he casts out demons by the Spirit of God and performs the acts without payment. John calls them signs. Historians differ: John P. Meier argues that the miracle traditions are too widely attested to be a later invention, while Paul J. Achtemeier notes that such acts were ambiguous even to eyewitnesses. Most scholars agree that he taught in parables and gathered followers. In Matthew and Luke Jesus also refuses a sign to a corrupt and evil generation except the sign of the prophet Jonah.
sections.opponents:
In the Gospels Jesus debates with Pharisees and Sadducees about how best to follow God. His critics found his ministry scandalous because he feasted with sinners, fraternized with women and allowed his followers to pluck grain on the Sabbath. When opponents say he casts out demons by Beelzebub, he answers that it would be illogical for Satan to undermine his own domain. Mark reports that his family came to take charge of him, saying he was out of his mind, and historians think this account is genuine because early Christians would hardly have invented it.

The Gospels report that a disciple, Judas Iscariot, agreed with the Jewish elders to betray him. E. P. Sanders doubts that disagreements about the Law would have led the authorities to want him killed. Many historians see political reasons. Pilate probably took talk of the Kingdom of God as a threat to Roman rule, and the Sadducean high priests may have seen Jesus as a danger to stability after he caused a disturbance in the Second Temple.

Scholars disagree on how far the Gospels preserve him. Some portray him as an apocalyptic preacher, others as a cynic sage, a charismatic healer or a prophet of social change. The Christ myth theory, that he never lived, is regarded as fringe, and virtually all scholars of antiquity accept that he existed.
sections.last:
All four Gospels describe a final week in Jerusalem. Jesus enters the city riding a young donkey, drives the money changers from the Temple, and shares the Last Supper with his twelve apostles, where he predicts a betrayal and, in the Synoptics, gives bread and wine as his body and blood. Judas then brings an armed crowd to Gethsemane and kisses him, and the disciples go into hiding. Peter denies knowing him three times.

The Gospels tell that he was brought before the high priest Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin, then before Pontius Pilate, who offered the crowd a choice between Jesus and Barabbas. Pilate had him scourged and sent him to be crucified at Calvary, also called Golgotha, with the sign Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Two thieves were crucified with him. Joseph of Arimathea buried him in a rock-hewn tomb. Astronomers have proposed 7 April 30 or 3 April 33 for the date, both Julian.

The Gospels do not describe the Resurrection itself but report an empty tomb and appearances, first to Mary Magdalene in Mark and John. Acts places the Ascension forty days later. The Quran holds that the Jews neither killed nor crucified him and that God raised him into the heavens; most classic Sunni and Twelver Shi'ite interpretations hold that his likeness was cast on a substitute.
sections.legacy:
Christians hold that through his death and resurrection people can be reconciled with God. The Resurrection became the foundation of the early Church, which grew into a worldwide movement. Most branches consider him God the Son, the second person of the Trinity, though Unitarians, Latter-day Saints and Jehovah's Witnesses are among the nontrinitarian groups. His birth is celebrated generally on 25 December as Christmas, his crucifixion on Good Friday and his resurrection on Easter Sunday. The most widely used calendar era is traditionally based on the approximate date of his birth.

Judaism rejects the belief that he was the awaited messiah, holding that he did not fulfil messianic prophecies, and Jewish tradition holds that he was neither divine nor resurrected. In Islam he is Isa, a messenger and the messiah, born of the virgin Mary but neither God nor the son of God, and mentioned by name 25 times in the Quran. Muslims believe he will return to Earth before the Day of Judgement. The Druze and the Baháʼí Faith also revere him.

Scholars of the historical Jesus have carried out three quests since the 18th century and still draw different portraits. The canonical texts, probably written between 50 and 120 CE, are the main sources historians use.

summary: Jesus was a Jewish preacher of Galilee and Judaea who taught about the Kingdom of God and was crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate. Christians hold him to be the Messiah and Son of God; historians study the Gospels' account critically, and other faiths give him other places.
references: E. P. Sanders, The Historical Figure of Jesus (Allen Lane Penguin Press, 1993)
Gerd Theissen, The Historical Jesus: A Comprehensive Guide (Fortress Press, 1998)
James D. G. Dunn, Jesus Remembered (Wm. B. Eerdmans, 2003)
Geza Vermes, Jesus the Jew: A Historian's Reading of the Gospels (First Fortress, 1981)
Bart Ehrman, Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium (Oxford University Press, 1999)
Robert E. Van Voorst, Jesus Outside the New Testament: An Introduction to the Ancient Evidence (Wm. B. Eerdmans, 2000)
notes: Birth c. 6 to 4 BC and death AD 30 or 33 as the article gives them; start -5 is the midpoint, end 30 the first of the two dates.
Ministry start c. 28 CE is the article's Luke/Tiberius estimate (28 or 29), other approaches 27 to 29.
The article places the Cleansing of the Temple at the end of the ministry in the Synoptics and the beginning in John; I told the Synoptic order.
Left out: the Magi, the flight to Egypt and the Transfiguration beyond a passing mention, for length.
